```{r}
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

## 

Identify the response variable type:

1. An online banking service must be able to determine whether or not a transaction being performed on the site is fraudulent, on the basis of the user’s IP address, past transaction history, and so forth.

. . .

## 

Identify the response variable type:

1. A marine biologist is trying to model the number of offspring sea otters have in an inlet in Monteray Bay, based on size of the mother and stability of environment.

. . .

2. An car insurance company is trying to predict if an applicat will have a car crash in the next 5 years, based on their income.

##

A **binary** variable is a categorical variable with only two levels

. . .

Can we model using linear regression?

##

Let's simulated data...

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(359)

n <- 300

sim_crash_data <- data.frame(
  #has_child = rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.4), 
  income = sample(25000:100000 / 1000, size = n, replace = TRUE) # Uniformly randomly samples
) |> 
  mutate(xb = -19 + 0.4 * income) |> 
  #mutate(xb2 = -19 - 2 * has_child + 0.4 * income) |> 
  mutate(pi =  1 / (1 + exp(-xb))) #|> 
  #mutate(has_child = ifelse(has_child == 1, yes = TRUE, no = FALSE))

sim_crash_data$car_crash <- sim_crash_data$pi |> 
  map_int(\(x) rbinom(n = 1, size = 1, prob = x))

```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "50%"
ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = car_crash)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Car crash"
  )
```

##

What does it mean to fit a line to this data?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "50%"
ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = car_crash)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Car crash"
  )
```

. . .

We don't get an error, but ...


## 

Linear regression assumes 
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + ... + \beta_p X_{pi} + \epsilon_i \text{ and } \epsilon_i\sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$

so 

$$E[Y_i | X_{1i}, ..., X_{pi}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + ... + \beta_p X_{pi}$$

. . .

What is the expectation of a binary variable?


##

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8

ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = pi)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Probability of car crash"
  )
```


## 

What is our expecation for people with an income of $45,000?

```{r}
crash_model <- lm(car_crash ~ income, data = sim_crash_data)

new_data <- data.frame(income = 45)

predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8
pred_45000 <- predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)

ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = pi)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(income = new_data$income, pi = pred_45000),
    color = "red",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Probability of car crash"
  )
```

## 

What is our expecation for people with an income of $90,000?

```{r}
crash_model <- lm(car_crash ~ income, data = sim_crash_data)

new_data <- data.frame(income = 90)

predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8
pred_90000 <- predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)

ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = pi)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(income = new_data$income, pi = pred_90000),
    color = "red",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Probability of car crash"
  )
```

Invalid probability! 

##

We can fit a linear model for a binary response, but:

- the line is really fitting the $E[Y_i|X_i]$, the probability
- the range of $E[Y_i|X_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + ... + \beta_p X_{pi}$ is $(-\infty, \infty)$
- we may get invalid predictions

. . .

We can use a logistic model instead!

##

The logistic function ranges from 0 to 1

$$logistic(Z) = \frac{e^Z}{1 + e^Z}$$

```{r}
data.frame(Z = seq(-10, 10, by = 0.01)) |> 
  mutate(logistic_Z = exp(Z) / (1 + exp(Z))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Z, y = logistic_Z)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Z", y = "Logistic(Z)")
```
